title: Schooldays, punishments and the red stage
author: Vijay  Shekhar
content_html:
Today’s children are more sensitive than children of previous generations. So much so that a stern word from a teacher seems like a major setback. But if we rewind the clock by 20 to 25 years, school life used to be an entirely different experience — an era when punishments were not rare exceptions, but woven into the daily fabric of school life.

Punishments used to be remarkably diverse. There were the relatively harmless ones like a sharp scolding, writing lines hundreds of times as an imposition or copying entire passages repeatedly. Then there were the stricter measures reserved for more disciplined classrooms by strict teachers on highly indisciplined students. A ruler across the knuckles was quite common, especially when a teacher expected absolute silence and unwavering attention.

One punishment that almost every Indian student from that era remembers is the classic sit-ups while holding one’s ears. Intended as a corrective measure, it often turned into an unexpected display of endurance, with students trying to outlast one another rather than feeling embarrassed.

Then there was that dreaded command, “Get out of the class!” Teachers often used this punishment when they wanted to remove a disruptive student without interrupting the lesson for everyone else. Standing outside the classroom came with its own set of challenges. The punishment was as much about public visibility as it was about discipline.

A student banished to the corridor instantly became a subject of curiosity. Other teachers passing by would take notice. And students from neighbouring classes, often on a conveniently timed trip to the restroom, would quickly spread the news. Before long, everyone seemed to know who had been thrown out of class and why.

But the greatest fear was the possibility of being spotted by the Principal or the Vice-Principal during one of their routine rounds. Such an encounter could easily escalate a minor classroom punishment into a much bigger problem, complete with explanations, warnings, and sometimes even a summons for the parents.

The red stage

The school I went to had (still has) something called the red stage. It was an area that was visible from every part (almost) of the school. It used to be the place for class photographs, announcements, open-air events and yes, for punishments too. Red stage punishments were beyond the ‘stand outside the classroom’ ones. These happened when a teacher really wanted the whole world (read ‘entire school’) to see the punished student(s). So much so that the red stage punishment became an aspirational ‘punishment band’ for many students.

I remember when I was in Class 11, a few of those ‘class bosses’ decided that it was an insult for the entire class that none of us had ever been punished on the red stage. They started planning for a ‘mass punishment’ on the red stage. But even in their mischievous endeavour, they had the good heart to keep the girl students out of this ‘mission’.

The opportunity came soon. We had a highly respected English teacher who one morning, before the first period started, brought a trunk full of Macbeth (part of our English Literature curriculum) props to the class with the help of two school support staffers. His class was the fourth or fifth period on that day. During the recess, the ‘bosses’ toppled the trunk and scattered its contents. Later in the day, when the teacher came to take his class and saw what had happened, he politely ‘thanked’ the students for what they did and walked out. Later the entire class, sans the girl students, was marched onto the red stage…and we all became certified ‘red stage punished’ students.

The decline

As the new millennium approached, attitudes toward discipline in schools began to change. Driven by the efforts of child welfare advocates, human rights organisations, educators and NGOs, corporal punishment and other forms of public humiliation increasingly came under scrutiny. Gradually practices that had once been considered routine became unacceptable, and schools were encouraged to adopt more constructive and child-friendly approaches to discipline.

title: The riddle of trauma
author: Cerin Pathrose
content_html:
Appa, you have any trauma from childhood?

The 150 kmph bouncer from my nine-year-old knocked me down. It took me some time to respond. Leave childhood, do I have any trauma? Nah! What’s the meaning of trauma? Is she really asking about “trauma”? I enquired, and she knew more than I expected her to.

I answered, I don’t have any trauma. She asked me to think again. No, I don’t have any. So I put the question back to her. And she shared hers.

In 2024, while we stopped at a fuel station in Tamil Nadu, a stray dog came running and started biting people there. Unfortunately, she was also attacked. She suffered a very small injury that didn’t even require hospital care. But to be cautious, we got her the rabies vaccine. She took multiple painful jabs around the wound. She cried loud in my hands. Yes, a harrowing time for her and us. We always knew that it had an impact on her. Her behaviour changed when a stray dog is around. We have two dogs at home. After this, she is more careful with them too. But I did not expect her to call that “trauma”.

Then I recalled a similar incident from my childhood in 1992 and shared with her. My cousin (about five years) and I (about 10) were taking our cattle out in the morning for grazing. It’s a regular chore for us in the holidays. My enthusiastic cousin playfully caned a calf, and there came the mother charging at him. He fell down, cow trying to gore him. I tried to stop the cow, holding to her horn and screaming for help. Luckily, he was saved by a dry stone wall; he fell close to it so the cow could not reach him properly. But he sustained an injury on his head which required seven painful stitches. He was deeply affected by the incident for a long time. He did not visit us for more than a year.

My daughter wondered about my cousin’s experience. We still have a cow at home. So she could relate. She was eager to see the scar on my cousin’s head. After all, she doesn’t have a scar from her encounter with dog!

Is this the “anxious generation” that Jonathan Haidt wrote a book on? Is a cocooned, predictable life stopping them from experiencing the uncertain world outside? Are they too soft and mild to face the real world? I don’t know.

I would prefer my child to be tough and not weighed down by her trauma. So, I reasoned with her that trauma is a word with much greater meaning and depth. What she experienced doesn’t quite classify as trauma. Yes, it is definitely an incident that she cannot forget. As she came out of it unscathed, it need not be identified as trauma. She seemed to understand.

I hope she reads about the harsher realities of world — famine, war, abuse, riots, and pogroms. Animals cannot cause any greater trauma than other humans.

title: A few kind words
author: Pushpanjali  Rout
content_html:
Sometimes, it is the smallest gestures that leave the biggest impact.

A few days ago, I bought a birthday card for a friend. Just a simple card with a handwritten note inside. To me, it felt natural. Growing up, birthday cards were a way of expressing feelings that we often struggled to say aloud.

What surprised me was the reaction it received.

When my friend’s other friends saw it, they were genuinely amazed. People still do this, they asked. They admired not just the card, but the effort behind it, the fact that someone had taken the time to choose a card, write a personal message, and make the occasion feel special.

Their appreciation made me realise something important: perhaps old-fashioned gestures never really go out of style. In a world of instant messages and quick reactions, thoughtful acts still have the power to touch hearts.

Then, something else happened that reinforced this thought even more.

Recently, I attended a Satyanarayan Puja. As I entered, I was speaking with my mother and preparing to offer flowers and seek blessings. In the middle of our conversation, a little girl, perhaps seven or eight years old, came running towards me.

At first, I was too engrossed in my conversation to understand what she wanted. But she persisted until she had my attention.

Then she said, “That day, you spoke so beautifully.”

For a moment, I was confused. Then I remembered.

A month earlier, I had done anchoring for our Odia community’s Utkal Divas celebration. It was my first time anchoring such an event. Many elders had appreciated my efforts, and I was grateful for their encouragement.

But hearing those words from a little child felt different.

There was something incredibly pure and genuine about it. She had remembered me after an entire month. She had remembered how I spoke. And she was excited enough to run across a crowded gathering just to tell me.

In that moment, I felt humbled, happy, and deeply touched.

It reminded me how powerful appreciation can be.

We often underestimate the impact of a compliment, a thank-you, or a few encouraging words. Yet those very words can lift someone’s mood, boost their confidence, and stay with them long after the moment has passed.

At the same time, they teach us another lesson: the opinions of jealous, critical, or negative people begin to matter far less when we focus on the kindness and encouragement around us.

A few sincere words from the right person can outweigh a hundred unnecessary opinions.

So perhaps the lesson is simple: write the card; give the compliment; appreciate someone’s effort; encourage the person who is trying.

You never know which small gesture will become a memory they carry with them for years. And sometimes, the encouragement you give may return to you when you least expect it from a friend, a stranger, or even a little child who simply wanted to say, “Didi, you spoke so beautifully.”

title: The 1990s experience
author: Ashok Balakrishna
content_html:
Change is normally greeted with inertia. But the 1990s children barely had that luxury. They have seen it all and more than that, they have chewed and savoured the saying, “Change is the only constant”. Being one among them, I had a life that so far had been like a train journey where you can’t help but embrace the change in motion, as you see changing terrains, landscapes, populace and so on.

Maybe, children of this generation, the famed Gen Zs, may not believe the things we say that existed 30 years ago. We would write letters in an inland cover and sometimes even in a postcard. I had preserved for a long time the letters I exchanged with a girlfriend of mine. We would wait for days to get a reply. Maybe that taught us some patience! Today, people get frustrated if they don’t get a reply in a few seconds or minutes.

Today’s children may not understand if we said we played all day out in the sun, fields, farms, plantations, and hills. That the games we played were all cheap thrills that sometimes came from dead wood, waste match boxes and cigarette packs, marbles and so on. The variety and the type of games we played was open to the creative extent as the games changed season wise, weather-wise and even day-wise. The marble itself offered us so many varieties of games and the winner would pride himself with a pocket full of clattering marbles.

Moreover, it was all with real friends and real world, nature, its trees and streams. That we plucked and ate fruits directly from the plants and trees and that itself is a travel theme now, to go “cherry-picking”, “self-harvesting”.

We used only a landline telephone and we didn’t know what a mobile was for a great amount of our growing-up years. TV itself was a luxury once and the whole village used to sit and watch a movie on a rented TV and VCR! The travelling theatre troupes were the only kind of concerts we had then. From VCRs, cassettes, Walkman sets, and CDs to the all-in-one phone era, the changes, if we sum up, is astounding and sometimes scary!

After dinner, the family would sit together outside on the verandah and chat as the children played in the moonlight. These family interactions itself is a luxury now, as everyone has a personal companion in hand. The grandparents’ house was the advance booked holiday resort for the entire summer and winter vacations unlike the resorts and home stays people spend a bomb to spend a day or two.

We grew up in a far secure world while our parents were too engaged to make ends meet. We grew up in a far cleaner, greener surroundings. Parents did not worry about which best school in the city to send us to. The government-run schools were all that we had and that sufficed.

We saw the technologies emerge, change, adapt or vanish. From letters to chat or date platforms, from DOS commands to conversational AI such as ChatGPT, we are the examples to show how technology came in like a lovely breeze but sucked in all of us like a tornado. Now, we realise that we are just in the middle and there is another half to expect a hurricane. Does that really excite or bother us? We really don’t know. We barely had leisure to think! We had to adopt and announce our arrival at every new platform! That wasn’t easy at all.

The world is really expected to change faster than it was so far. The human brain once starved for food, but not any more. Knowledge is an open source now and the children of this generation as we see are far more confident and innovative and aren’t ready to accept a mediocre life! But sometimes too much light is blinding and they may need us to guide them in the right light. And for that we still need to keep pace with the changing technologies and be abreast and upbeat! Cheers to those 1990s and cheers to whatever that future holds for.
